turn_text: I think the Senate Democrats have demonstrated that with even a razor thin majority, they have the capacity to drive serious legislative content forward. What they're not going to have is the option of reconciliation. I think as the Republican selection of a speaker settles down and as committees are chosen, you're going to see the House, which is going to become an effective barrier in a lot of respect to major legislative initiatives from the left. You're also going to see a potential for a rethinking of the house as a legislative body. For too long, basically a strong speaker system has existed that has allowed Nancy Pelosi and others to function effectively as a lot of crowds. That is not the way the political culture of the house has drifted in recent years. And I think what you're likely to see is a couple of things. One, I think there will be legislative activity this year, but it's not going to be big ideological initiatives. What it is going to be is technical improvements, corrections, and small ball legislation done within committees with a certain amount of bipartisan participation, and then rolled out on the floor of the House. There are a couple of obvious places to look for this to happen, with GT Thompson of Pennsylvania as the new chairman of the Agriculture Committee, GT is going to be doing a farm bill, and although there's been some skepticism, I think there is a bipartisan base there to put together a working farm bill that can pass in this Congress. I think you're also going to see, you're probably not going to see a budget pass, both houses, although you have Mr. Boyle, and Mr. Spock are both in critical positions in the house on this. What you're likely to see is two very different budget authorities developed for each house and then kind of wave through. So in terms of a response to the budget and to appropriations, you're going to see very difficult different results in the Senate and in the house. You're also going to see I think some very interesting opportunities to sharpen legislation and develop it in some areas that have been neglected. For example, I think you're going to see Mr. Kelly of Northwestern, Pennsylvania, cheering a subcommittee of the Ways and Means Committee with the opportunity to seriously develop new tax legislation and work through the details. What we've had for the past couple of sessions has been severe ideological friction and partisan differences. What I think you have the potential to see now is at the committee level, below the level of leadership, the opportunity for some bipartisan interaction, and with Pennsylvanians playing a critical role in making that happen. So I'm telling people that I'm working with to look for strategies to move issues at the committee level and be prepared to develop champions on both sides of the aisle because bipartisanship is going to be necessary to move legislation forward.

I think we trail all those countries and the EU in terms of trade agreements with other countries. And we're losing opportunity. Pennsylvania companies, we've shown when they have the opportunity to compete with with, you know, around the globe, they succeed. But we need, you know, we need good trade agreements that promote fair and free trade in order to do that. And certainly hope it is a priority going into the next couple of years.

turn_text: The other big issue, of course, is the World Trade Organization, which has fallen on, I think, rough times. I think the participation in the world trading system by the United States is facilitated when you have a strong rules-based trading system. And what we're seeing right now is a bifurcation where increasingly we have countries that are aligned with us that are following the same general rules And at the same time, we are seeing organized more and more around China, another axis that approaches trade in a very different way. And increasingly, I think, a mutually exclusive way. And that is going to be one of the most difficult nuts that this administration in the next few is going to have to crack. The World Trade Organization is going to have to be rethought if it's going to be the center of a rules-based trading system. I think that we allowed China into the WTO when I was in Congress. And we had no notion at the time that China at this stage would still be insisting on being treated as a developing economy, essentially dictating for itself a series of exclusions from the rules that the developed world is required to follow. That is precisely the kind of inequity that needs to be rethought. And if we're going to have a strong rules-based trading system, there needs to be an accepted rule keeper that's able to make decisions that countries will abide by. That means the WTO is going to have to be reformed or replaced.

Democrats on election night won a very narrow majority, 102 to 101, first majority for the Democratic Party in over a decade. But soon thereafter, they became a functional minority, the unfortunate unfortunate death of a state representative Tony DeLuca out in Allegheny County, a couple members of the House Democratic Caucus elected to higher offices. So when the election for Speaker of the House came up, it was 101 Republicans, 299 Democrats, and certainly not clear how that election was going to play out. Joanna McClinton from Philadelphia, the Democratic leader was viewed as the front runner for Speaker of the House, but not necessarily a clear path to get there, given how the votes were shaking out. Brian Cutler, the former Speaker of the House from Lancaster County and the Republican leader sort of viewed as the Republican alternative. Ultimately, when the final vote came up, neither of them were part of that election. two names that had really not been discussed much at all were on that, you know, in the final vote. On the Republican side, you had State Representative Carl Metzger from Somerset County, and on the Democratic side, State Representative Mark Rossi from Berks County, and Representative Rossi all ultimately won the election as Speaker of the House for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, with the coalition vote of all the Democrats and about 15 or so Republicans, including Republican leadership, who voted for Mark Rossi.
